archetype.name: Rebuilding (run-first, defense in freefall)
archetype.definition: A first-year staff with a 1-8 record, the league's least efficient defense and an injured starting quarterback, whose real job for the rest of the year is learning who belongs in the next version of the team.

report.headline: A competitive loser with the league's worst defense, now without its quarterback.
report.take:
Miami is not a good team hiding behind bad luck. The point differential implies about two wins, the record shows one, and winsOverExpected of -1.03 says a bounce or two went the wrong way. That is a rounding error, not a hidden contender. Net EPA ranks 30th, the defense ranks dead last in EPA allowed and success rate allowed, and the offense sits 29th in success rate. The history explains the arc: an 11-win, top-five-offense team in 2023 slid to 8 wins, then 7, and the defense went from 8th in EPA allowed in 2024 to 25th last year to 32nd now. Jeff Hafley inherited a declining roster, not a broken-luck one.

The identity is clear. Hafley's offense runs far more than the situation calls for, with a pass rate over expected of -8.5 (31st). The line produces strange run numbers: 2.99 yards before contact ranks 3rd, but the stuff rate ranks 30th, so the ground game is boom-or-bust. It shows up as 217 rushing yards against Cincinnati and 74 against New England a few weeks later. Malik Willis's passing was just as streaky, from -10 pass EPA in Minnesota to +10.5 in the win over the Jets. The constant was a pocket under siege, with a sack rate that ranks 30th.

The numbers hide some progress. After two September blowouts against San Francisco and Kansas City, Miami played almost everyone close. It lost by five in Minnesota, seven to Cincinnati, five to New England and two in Indianapolis, and covered most of those spreads. The defense also limits yardage better than its efficiency suggests: 13th in yards allowed per game, but 29th on third down. Drives keep moving just enough, and the defense has made 12 sacks (31st) and 7 takeaways (29th) to stop them.

The next stretch gets harder. Willis is on IR with an abdominal injury and a surgery decision still pending; the estimate is mid-December. Center Aaron Brewer is out with a concussion, and DT Zeek Biggers is done for the year. Kyle McCord kept it close in Indianapolis with -8.3 pass EPA and help from two takeaways. That is not a formula that travels to Buffalo.

strengths.title: Takes away the top two receivers
strengths.body: Opposing WR1s and WR2s have scored well below their usual output against Miami, both ranking 3rd in the league. The outside coverage is the one part of the defense doing its job, and it keeps yards allowed in the top half of the league. It is real but narrow: offenses have simply moved the ball to the slot and tight end instead.

strengths.title: Line creates early running room
strengths.body: Miami's backs average 2.99 yards before contact, 3rd in the league, and short-yardage conversion ranks 10th. That gives Hafley's run-heavy plan something real to build on, and it can shorten games against better teams. The catch is the 30th-ranked stuff rate: the runs that don't hit are dead on arrival, which keeps overall run EPA in the bottom third.

strengths.title: Competitive since September
strengths.body: After losing by double digits to San Francisco and Kansas City, Miami lost one-score games to Minnesota, New England and Indianapolis and beat the Jets. It covered in several of those weeks even as an underdog. That reflects a run-and-shorten-the-game approach more than true quality, but it makes the Dolphins a frustrating out.

concerns.title: Defense can't get off the field
concerns.body: Miami ranks 32nd in EPA allowed and 32nd in success rate allowed, with 31st in pass EPA allowed and 29th on third down. The leaks are over the middle: the defense is the league's worst against tight ends and slot receivers by EPA per target. A weak pass rush (12 sacks, 31st) means quarterbacks have time to find them. Losing DT Biggers for the season makes the front thinner, so this is structural rather than variance.

concerns.title: Pocket breaks down, QB is gone
concerns.body: Miami allows pressure at a 28th-ranked rate and sacks at a 30th-ranked rate. Time to throw ranks among the longest in the league, so the quarterback holding the ball is part of it, not just the line. Now Willis is on IR, starting center Brewer is out, and McCord's first start produced -8.3 pass EPA. Expect the passing game to get worse before it gets better.

concerns.title: Special teams give away field
concerns.body: Miami's special teams cost it 2.7 EPA a game, 28th in the league. For a team that wins only by shortening games and staying close, hidden yardage in the kicking game is the kind of margin it cannot afford. It has been consistent enough to treat as a real flaw.

trend.note: Margins tightened after the September blowouts, with five straight one-score finishes from Week 4 on except Detroit, but the losses kept coming. The quarterback switch to McCord in Week 10 kept it close in Indianapolis on takeaways, not passing.

nextGame.headline: Backup quarterback, backup center, and the league's top offense waiting.
nextGame.body:
Buffalo is 8-1 and the Book makes Miami a 16.5-point underdog (+800) with a 45.5 total. The Bills have the league's best offense by EPA and points, and a running game that ranks 1st in success rate behind a line that rarely gets stuffed. That is a bad meeting for a Miami defense that ranks last in success allowed. The Bills are not flawless, though. Their defense ranks 29th in EPA allowed and 30th in missed tackles, and their 8-1 record leans on close wins (0.8 one-score win rate, +1.7 wins over expected). A patient running team can find yards against them. The early forecast shows gusts near 27 mph; if that holds it would favor Miami's ground plan and drag on the total, but it is too far out to lean on.

Availability tilts hard toward Buffalo. Miami starts McCord again with Willis on IR, plays without center Brewer, WR Chris Bell and WR Jared Wayne, and has lost DT Biggers for the season with DT Jordan Phillips questionable. That leaves the interior run defense thin against the league's most efficient rushing attack. Buffalo's issues are in the secondary: CBs Christian Benford and Dee Alford are both questionable after leaving their last game. That matters because the Bills already give opposing WR1s more than almost anyone.

waysToWin.title: Washington against a thin secondary
waysToWin.body: Buffalo lets opposing WR1s score well above their usual output, 30th in the league. Benford and Alford are both questionable. Malik Washington, Miami's clear target leader, is the one receiver who can make McCord's job simple. Quick, defined throws to him also beat the rush before it arrives.

waysToWin.title: Grind clock, shrink the game
waysToWin.body: Miami already runs far more than expected, and Buffalo's defense is middling against the run (18th in rush EPA allowed) and 30th in missed tackles. Long drives that end in points keep Josh Allen's offense on the sideline. If the wind is real, it pushes the game further toward the ground. That is how Miami stayed close to Minnesota and Indianapolis.

waysToWin.title: Cash in on Buffalo's sloppiness
waysToWin.body: The Bills commit 8.6 penalties a game (30th) and run a negative turnover margin. The two takeaways in Indianapolis kept McCord's start alive. An upset at +800 likely needs short fields and drive-extending flags.

waysToLose.title: Pass rush swallows a makeshift pocket
waysToLose.body: Buffalo generates pressure at the 2nd-highest rate in the league. Miami allows sacks at the 30th-ranked rate and will be without its starting center, with a backup quarterback behind them. Drive-killing sacks and forced throws are the most likely way this gets out of hand early.

waysToLose.title: Bills run through a depleted interior
waysToLose.body: Buffalo's rushing offense leads the league in success rate. Miami allows the highest success rate on defense and just lost Biggers, with Phillips questionable. If the Bills can stay on schedule on the ground, the third-down problems (29th) become a long afternoon.

waysToLose.title: Tight ends and slot over the middle
waysToLose.body: Miami is the league's worst defense against tight ends and slot receivers by EPA per target. Buffalo's passing offense ranks 4th by EPA. Even if Miami's corners hold up outside, Allen has an easy, repeatable answer inside.

nextGame.watch: How fast McCord gets the ball out against Buffalo's pass rush with a backup center snapping. If Miami can't stay ahead of the chains, the run-first plan collapses.

restOfSeason.body:
The schedule offers two real chances, the Jets at home and the Chargers at home, between road trips to Denver and Green Bay, a visit from Chicago and two more Buffalo/New England division games. A defense this inefficient, now missing a starting DT, will not suddenly improve. The offense's floor depends on Willis's recovery: the mid-December estimate is soft until a surgery decision is made. Expect more close-but-losing games against mid-tier opponents, a couple of lopsided ones against the good offenses, and roughly two or three wins total.

What holds: the run-first identity, the ability to shorten games, and solid coverage on the outside. What won't: anything built on McCord turning negative passing EPA into points, or takeaway-driven covers like Indianapolis. If Willis returns healthy for the final month, the offense should look more like the Jets win than the Detroit loss.
swingFactors: Timing and health of Willis's return
Interior defensive line depth after Biggers

confidence.note: The team's true level is clear over nine games, but the QB and center injuries make the next month hard to pin down.
